Stage 3b: external, fiscal and financial blocks

Three blocks added one at a time — what each cost, which one broke things, and a fourth failed attempt at the import price

1. What each block cost

Blocks were added cumulatively, with the full diagnostic battery after each, so it is visible which one degrades what. The baseline is stage 3a phase A.

Cumulative cost of each block. T = 98 throughout.
step k df signs acceptance_flagged mean_ci_width
stage 3a (baseline) 83 15 20/20 0 1.230
+ external 84 14 20/21 0 1.240
+ fiscal 88 10 22/23 0 1.616
+ financial 90 8 26/30 0 1.863

The degrees-of-freedom arithmetic was predicted before estimating and matched exactly. The fiscal block is the expensive one: its accumulation identity carries a lagged term, and its government-consumption equation takes a lagged GDP term, so it costs four columns where the others cost one and two.

2. The fiscal block had to be reduced, and the reason is data, not design

The request specified revenue and expenditure equations with de_deficit == de_expenditure - de_revenue. That block cannot be estimated: German quarterly revenue and expenditure (Eurostat gov_10q_ggnfa) begin 2002Q1, and T is system-wide, so pulling them in shortens the estimation window for every equation from 98 to 90 while k rises to 90 — leaving zero residual degrees of freedom.

fiscal variant k T df
as specified (revenue + expenditure) 90 90 0
as built (Maastricht debt) 88 98 10

The block is therefore built on gov_10q_ggdebt (GD, percent of GDP), which is clean 2000Q1–2026Q1 for all eleven economies. What is lost is the revenue/expenditure decomposition. What is kept is the mechanism the request called out as mattering: debt accumulates, and the sovereign spread responds to it.

de_netborrowing is not the headline deficit, and no coefficient on it should be read as a deficit elasticity. It is the quarterly change in the debt ratio, which is the deficit plus the growth-denominator effect plus stock-flow adjustments. It is derived that way deliberately: it makes the accumulation identity exact by construction (verified below), and it sets the carry weight to exactly 1, which matters because koma’s injected weights are not time-varying — they are annualised, lagged a year and collapsed to a single scalar — so a genuine (1+i)/(1+g) snowball factor could not have been expressed as a weight at all.

3. Two koma limitations found on the way

Both would have caused silent damage rather than an error.

A lagged identity could not be built. koma supports one — its own Klein vignette ships capital_stock == 1.001*capital_stock.L(1) + 0.0002*investment — but stage2_exogenous_variables() collected identity component names raw, so de_govdebt.L(1) was declared exogenous while koma strips the suffix on its side and rejects the leftover as “Redundant exogenous variables detected”. Fixed by stripping .L(...), as the preflight already did.

Lagged endogenous names must not prefix one another. koma’s construct_phi() locates a variable’s lag columns with an unanchored grepl(paste0("^", name), ...). With both de_debt.L(1) and de_debt_ratio.L(1) present, the shorter name matches both, the inner loop runs twice for the same lag order, and the second pass overwrites the first — pointing the companion matrix at the wrong row of B, with no error and no warning. The names here (de_govdebt, de_netborrowing) share no prefix, and stage2_preflight() gained an eighth check so it cannot be reintroduced.

A third, smaller trap: an identity term written without an explicit weight (b == b.L(1) + d) is stored with character(0) weights — the same silent corruption CLAUDE.md records for + -0.4*x. identity_equation() always emits 1*x, so building identities through it stays safe.

4. Block 1 — external

The external block’s equations.
equation term estimate ci_low ci_high
de_exports de_exports.L(1) 0.253 -0.138 0.667
de_exports de_foreign_demand 1.967 -0.678 4.693
de_exports de_competitiveness -1.257 -2.699 0.247
de_imports de_imports.L(1) 0.221 -0.226 0.634
de_imports de_domestic_demand 0.470 -1.118 2.285
de_current_account de_current_account.L(1) 0.972 0.890 1.047
de_current_account de_exports 0.068 -0.046 0.150
de_current_account de_imports -0.044 -0.157 0.069
de_current_account de_terms_of_trade 0.079 -0.168 0.316

The competitiveness restriction worked as intended. Stage 3a estimated the two export-price terms separately and got −0.92 and +1.26 with both intervals wide and spanning zero — the data did not reject equal-and-opposite, and did not identify them apart either. Imposing the difference trades two poorly-identified coefficients for one, and that one comes back correctly signed. The current account’s own equation behaves: it rises with exports, falls with imports, and improves with the terms of trade.

4.1 A fourth failed attempt at the import price

The one substantive failure is de_imports ← de_terms_of_trade, and it is the fourth specification to fail in the same direction.

Every attempt to give German import volumes a price term. The last row’s implied coefficient is -1 times the terms-of-trade coefficient, since ToT enters import prices negatively.
specification domestic_demand implied_import_price
no price term (adopted in 3a) 0.524 NA
own price, contemporaneous 0.078 0.695
own price + domestic price 0.027 0.799
own price, lagged 0.386 0.401
inside terms of trade (3b) 0.470 NA

Terms of trade is export_prices − import_prices, so a coefficient of NA on it implies NA on import prices — the same positive sign as the direct contemporaneous term, and the same sign as every other attempt. Four specifications, one contamination: within a quarter, German import volumes and German import prices both respond to the same global impulse, and the equation contains no control for world activity (foreign_demand sits on the export side) to separate them.

The terms-of-trade version does damage the demand elasticity less than the bare own price did (0.47 against 0.08), so it is the least bad of the four — but it is still wrong-signed, and being least-bad is not a reason to keep a coefficient that says import demand rises when imports get expensive.

Recommendation: drop the terms-of-trade term from the imports equation, as was done in stage 3a for the direct price. Terms of trade would remain in the system for the current-account equation, where it is correctly signed and where a relative price genuinely belongs. This is a change to the block as approved, so it is reported rather than applied.

5. Block 2 — fiscal

The fiscal block’s equations.
equation term estimate ci_low ci_high
de_government constant 0.540 0.044 1.057
de_government de_government.L(1) -0.109 -0.672 0.425
de_government de_gdp.L(1) -0.168 -0.456 0.148
de_netborrowing constant -0.074 -1.357 1.258
de_netborrowing de_netborrowing.L(1) 0.334 -0.369 1.002
de_netborrowing de_long_rate 0.068 -0.351 0.443
de_netborrowing de_gdp -0.254 -0.729 0.265

Both fiscal sign rules pass. Net borrowing falls when output grows (automatic stabilisers) and rises with the long rate (debt service), though both intervals span zero — at this sample length the signs are right and the magnitudes are not pinned down.

de_government correctly has no Metropolis step: both its regressors are lagged, so its gamma block is empty and count_accepted is NA. That is deliberate. Letting government consumption respond to contemporaneous output would build in a within-quarter automatic stabiliser this data cannot identify, and would put a policy variable inside the simultaneous block.

5.1 The accumulation identity is exact, and does not destabilise the lags

Debt accumulation and lag stability.
check value
govdebt == govdebt.L(1) + netborrowing, max |residual| 0
own lags with |coefficient| >= 1 0
largest own lag 0.9986 (de_unemployment)

The debt ratio’s law of motion holds exactly, and nothing became explosive. This was the stated worry — a near-unit-root accumulation entering a system whose largest own lag was already 0.9999 — and it did not materialise. The reason is structural rather than lucky: de_govdebt is an identity with a fixed unit weight, not an estimated equation, so the unit root is imposed exactly at 1 and cannot be drawn above it. What could still destabilise the system is the loop the accumulation sits in, which is section 6’s business.

5.2 On its own, the fiscal block transmits nothing

The debt stock is terminal until the financial block arrives.
question answer
equations taking de_govdebt contemporaneously, at the fiscal step none

This is worth stating plainly because it is the honest reading of the per-block table: the fiscal block is pure cost until the financial block lands. It spends four columns of k and widens every credible interval in the system by about a quarter, and until de_long_rate takes de_govdebt there is no equation for the debt stock to influence — the same terminal-variable pathology CLAUDE.md records for long_rate in stage 2 and for export_prices in stage 3a. The two blocks have to be judged together, not separately.

6. Block 3 — financial

The financial block was estimated twice. The first attempt modelled the long rate as a level and broke the system; the second models the spread and mostly repairs it. Both are shown, because the failure is the more instructive half.

6.1 The level specification broke the long-rate equation

de_long_rate under the level specification. The own lag is stable for three systems, then crosses 1 exactly when de_govdebt is added.
step own_lag policy_rate govdebt
stage 3a 0.9255 0.0600 NA
+ external 0.9387 0.0450 NA
+ fiscal 0.9183 0.0689 NA
+ financial (LEVEL) 1.0038 -0.0257 -0.0058

The own lag sat at 0.92–0.94 for three consecutive systems, then jumped to 1.004 — explosive — the moment de_govdebt became its fifth regressor at df = 8, with the policy-rate loading flipping negative at the same instant. At that point the equation was no longer identified: the lag ran to a unit root and absorbed the structural content, leaving the debt coefficient at −0.006 and dragging down everything that loads on the long rate. Seven sign checks failed.

6.2 Modelling the spread repairs most of it

de_spread    ~ de_govdebt + de_gdp + de_spread.L(1)
de_long_rate == 1*de_spread + 1*ea_policy_rate

This imposes the policy-rate coefficient at 1 rather than estimating it, removes the unit root (a spread is stationary where a rate level is not), and cuts the competing regressors from five to three. It costs nothing in degrees of freedom — the long rate loses its own lag column and the spread gains one.

Level versus spread.
quantity level_spec spread_spec
own lag of the modelled rate 1.0038 (explosive) 0.8894
coefficient on de_govdebt -0.0058 (wrong sign) +0.0151 (correct sign)
policy-rate coefficient -0.0257 (estimated, wrong sign) 1.0000 (imposed by the identity)
failing sign checks 7 4

The explosive lag is gone, the policy-rate coefficient is imposed rather than mis-estimated, and the debt coefficient changes sign to the one the economics requires. sovereign_spread_widens_with_debt now passes.

6.3 But the debt channel is still weak, and the credit channel is wrong

The spread equation.
equation term estimate ci_low ci_high
de_spread de_spread.L(1) 0.8894 0.5124 1.2692
de_spread de_gdp -0.0132 -0.2167 0.1585
de_spread de_govdebt 0.0151 -0.0294 0.0666
Remaining failures.
check equation term estimate expected
wage_price_indexation_in_0_1 de_wages de_prices -0.0059 in (0, 1)
price_phillips_curve_negative de_nonenergy_prices de_unemployment 0.0040 < 0
credit_rises_with_output de_credit de_gdp -0.0196 > 0
investment_rises_with_credit de_investment de_credit -0.1686 > 0

Two things should temper the improvement:

  • The debt coefficient’s interval still straddles zero. The sign is right; the magnitude is not identified. “Correctly signed but indistinguishable from zero” is an honest description of the sovereign-spread channel in this fit, and it is weaker than the block’s premise requires.
  • The credit channel does not work. Credit falls in output rather than rising, and investment falls in credit rather than rising. These are the financial block’s own economics, not collateral damage from the long rate, and they do not have a specification fix waiting the way the spread did.

The other two failures — wage indexation at −0.006 and the price Phillips curve at +0.004 — are the same near-zero pair that trades places between runs. Both have intervals an order of magnitude wider than their estimates; they are sampling noise on weak coefficients rather than findings.

7. Verdict

Per-block verdict.
block cost_df verdict
external 1 Keep. The competitiveness restriction works and the current account behaves; near-zero cost in precision.
fiscal 4 Keep, but only with the financial block. Correct signs, exact identity, no destabilisation – yet it costs 24% of the system’s precision and on its own de_govdebt reaches no equation at all.
financial 2 Weakest of the three, and improved rather than fixed. The spread reformulation removed the explosive lag and corrected the debt sign, but the debt channel stays indistinguishable from zero and the credit channel is wrong-signed.

Which block breaks things: the financial one — and the reason was identification, not economics. The level specification put a fifth regressor on an equation already carrying a near-unit-root lag at df = 8; the lag won. Modelling the spread instead recovered most of what was lost at zero cost in degrees of freedom, which is worth remembering as a general lesson: when a coefficient goes null, check whether a neighbouring lag has gone to a unit root and swallowed it before concluding the channel is absent.

What survives. The external block is close to free and works. The fiscal block is sound in isolation and delivers an exact accumulation identity without destabilising anything — the stated worry about a near-unit-root stock did not materialise, because an identity with a fixed unit weight cannot be drawn above one. The sovereign-spread channel exists and points the right way, but is not sharply identified.

What does not. The credit channel: credit falls in output, investment falls in credit. Unlike the spread, this has no obvious specification fix, and at df = 8 with intervals 51% wider than the stage-3a baseline it is not clear the data can support the block at all.

On the import price, now 4 for 4. Direct (+0.70), with a domestic counterpart (+0.80), lagged (+0.40), and inside terms of trade (implied +0.91). Every specification puts a positive coefficient on import prices in the volume equation. The term is dropped; terms of trade remains in the current-account equation, where it is correctly signed.

Eight-quarter forecast

8 quarters from 2025Q1 to 2026Q4, 1000 posterior draws. Actuals exist for the first 5 quarters; the rest is genuinely ahead of the data.

Every fan below is the filtered predictive interval: koma constrains no draw to be stationary, so a draw whose quarterly growth exceeds 100% in absolute value is dropped before the quantiles are taken, exactly as score_forecast() does when it scores a backtest. The solid band is the 25th-75th percentile of what survives, the faint band the 10th-90th, the dark line their median, and the grey line the realised path where one exists. Across the variables shown, 5.1% of draws are discarded as explosive at horizon 1, rising to 42.4% at horizon 8 (worst: ie_gdp at 83.8%). A variable whose discarded share climbs steeply is one whose fan understates the model’s true uncertainty, so read the tail of a wide fan as an ordering rather than a number.

The panels are clipped, and that is worth saying plainly. Eight quarters out, the 10-90 interval on quarterly growth spans tens of percentage points in every stage of this project – an honest number, and one that makes the median invisible if the axis is scaled to contain it. Each panel is therefore scaled to its inner band, and the outer band runs to the panel edge rather than being drawn in full. Nothing is concealed: the table at the end of this section reports the untruncated bounds.

Every level path is anchored on an observed value (largest anchor discrepancy 0.00%, on at_imports), so the level and rate charts are both directly comparable to the actuals.

A forecast this long needs the exogenous series to reach the end of the horizon, and they do not: every one of them stops at the fit’s own native forecast end. extend_forecast_horizon() carries each one forward on its trailing four-quarter average growth – a momentum continuation, not a view on oil markets or world trade – and koma would otherwise have silently returned a shorter horizon than the one requested.
